newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Alternative Living sees a profit in FY97.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Alternative Living sees a profit in FY97.

text.p: Alternative Living Services Inc expects to reap benefits from its growth strategy and turn a profit by the end of 1997, a company official said.

"As that growth continues to get stronger and our infrastructure is funded by operations... we will break even by mid-year and be a profitable company by the end of the year," Bill Lasky, the company's chief executive officer, told Reuters in an interview Friday.
The Brookfield, Wisconsin-based company currently operates 79 assisted living centers in 11 states, Lasky said.

On Thursday, Alternative Living reported a loss of $1.6 million or $0.12 a share for the fourth quarter ended December 31, compared to a loss of $696,000 or $0.09 a share a year ago when the company operated 19 centers.
The company said operating expenses totaled $15.2 million versus $3.6 million in the corresponding period in 1995.
"Financial results were precisely what management and analysts expectations were set out to be," Lasky said.
"Even though we are a health care service business," he explained, "we need to construct hundreds of millions of dollars worth of real estate to provide this service."
Alternative Living has 26 facilities under construction, 44 projects under development and 25 additional facilities scheduled to break ground over the next 60 days, Lasky said.
Lasky said the company expects to have capacity for 5,600 residents and revenue of just above $100 million for 1997.
Gregory Moerschel, an analyst for ABN AMRO Chicago Corp, said he expects the company to report revenues of $103 million for 1997, and earnings per share of $0.10 for the year.
"We're projecting breakeven in late June, and a profit by the September quarter," he said."

"Greg's expectations are very similar to (estimates by) other analysts that cover the company," Lasky said. "Those expectations match well with what we expect to do with moving the company out of a loss to breakeven by mid-year and then starting to turn profitable."
"This is simply the result of the tremendous growth we had in 1996 and the strong construction pipeline and development we're coming through in 1997," Lasky said.
